questions.question: Explain why soil is treated as a non-renewable resource, and discuss the human, animal and physical causes of soil erosion in South Africa, including the role of the past.
questions.expected_answer: A few centimetres of topsoil take several hundred years to form under African conditions — weathering, plant growth, decay and soil organisms working slowly — while a single storm on bare ground can strip more than that in an afternoon, so on any human timescale lost soil does not return. Physical causes are the agents themselves: water eroding in the sequence splash, sheet, rill and gully, and wind lifting dry, bare soil; steep slopes, intense Highveld thunderstorms and drought cycles make South Africa naturally erosion-prone, but physical agents mostly finish what land use starts, because bare ground is the precondition. Human causes make the ground bare: overcultivation exhausting humus, ploughing up and down slopes so furrows become drains, deforestation for timber and firewood, mining and construction exposing raw surfaces. Animal causes centre on overgrazing — stock stripping grass faster than it regrows — and trampling, which compacts paths so water runs off rather than soaking in; cattle tracks often become the starter channels of gullies. The past matters: apartheid's homeland system concentrated too many people and animals on the smallest, poorest land with insecure tenure, engineering the overuse whose scars — the Eastern Cape's dongas — remain, while present-day poverty, firewood dependence and population growth keep pressure on land already wounded.

questions.question: Describe the evidence of soil erosion in South Africa and its effects on both people and the environment.
questions.expected_answer: Evidence: dongas — steep-sided gullies deep enough to swallow a vehicle — cut through parts of the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Limpopo, especially former homeland districts; rivers run brown after storms because the colour is topsoil in transit; dams silt up, with the Welbedacht Dam on the Caledon River losing most of its storage capacity within decades of construction; and dust plumes, exposed roots and fence posts standing on pedestals of soil complete the picture, with the country losing an estimated several hundred million tonnes of topsoil per year. Effects on people: yields fall as the fertile layer thins, shrinking farm incomes and raising food prices; rural livelihoods collapse where cropland and grazing degrade, pushing migration to towns; dam siltation shortens the life of water storage that cities and irrigation depend on; and fertiliser must expensively replace the free fertility that washed away. Effects on the environment: rivers and wetlands choke with sediment, smothering aquatic life; the land's ability to absorb and slowly release water declines, sharpening floods and weakening dry-season flows; degraded veld carries less biodiversity; and at the extreme, erosion tips into desertification. The summary: a slow-motion disaster in which no single storm makes headlines, but the cumulative loss undermines food security, water security and rural livelihoods at once.

questions.question: Discuss the management strategies used to prevent and control soil erosion, and explain the GIS concepts — spatially referenced data, spatial and spectral resolution, and point, line and area data — as applied to erosion management.
questions.expected_answer: Prevention keeps soil covered and anchored: contour ploughing runs furrows along the slope so each ridge dams runoff instead of channelling it; strip cropping alternates cover and row crops; crop rotation and fallow rebuild humus; mulching and stubble keep fields covered between seasons; windbreaks slow erosive wind; and on grazing land, stock numbers are matched to the veld's carrying capacity with camps rested in rotation and watering routes managed to spread trampling. Control repairs existing damage: check dams and gabions — rock-packed wire baskets — cross gullies to slow water and trap sediment so the floor rises and vegetation re-establishes; raw surfaces are replanted and healing land fenced off, with national programmes like LandCare, Working for Water and Working on Fire carrying these measures to scale. The GIS toolkit: spatially referenced data is information tied to coordinates — a gully's position, a rainfall station's reading. Spatial resolution is the ground size of one pixel, deciding whether a sensor sees fields or only regions; spectral resolution is which wavelength bands are recorded, and because healthy vegetation reflects infrared strongly, infrared bands expose bare and stressed ground early. Features are stored as point data (a borehole or gully head), line data (rivers, contours, fences) and area or polygon data (fields, catchments, risk zones); overlaying slope, rainfall, soil and vegetation layers maps where erosion risk concentrates, directing scarce resources — such as gabion-building teams — to the highest-risk valleys first.
